newsitem.title: GERMANY: Stable German prices show inflation under control.
newsitem.headline: Stable German prices show inflation under control.

text.p: Stable preliminary figures for west German inflation for October show prices in the federal republic are under control and that monetary policy should remain on hold for the time being, analysts said on Thursday.
The closely-monitored west German consumer price index registered no change from September, while the year-on-year increase was only 1.5 percent.

Ulf Rassat, economist at Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechsel Bank in Munich, said: "We think prices will stay stable until winter -- they certainly won't decrease. Most of the impact from oil prices is already in there, and we we've factored in a slight increase in CPI for November and December."

The initial tranche of CPI data came from the state statistics office in Hesse and it set the tone for the day's reports, showing that October consumer prices rose only 1.3 percent year-on-year and were unchanged month-on-month.
Later, the southern state of Baden-Wuerttemberg said prices were also unchanged on the month and rose 1.3 percent on the year.

"We are very happy with the figures from Hesse and Baden-Wuerttemberg, and the figures were within our expectations. The figures are fully on target," said Manuela Preuschl, an economist with DB Research in Frankfurt.
Later in the day, the North Rhine-Westphalian palatinate came out with its data, which showed a rise of 0.1 percent month-on-month and 1.6 percent on an annual basis.
This was followed by data from Bavaria, which showed CPI unchanged on a monthly basis and up 1.4 percent year-on-year.
Elanie Heldmann at BfG Bank in Frankfurt said the inflation figures were positive, if a little higher than she had been expecting, but that they limited scope for the Bundesbank to cut rates.

"The figures suggest a decent price environment. It leaves the Bundesbank in a good position to leave rates where they are. There is no real reason for a cut in short-term interest rates. All in all, a positive development," said Heldmann.
Rassat said: "These figures all suggest stability and we don't think they will have any impact on interest rates."

Economists had been worried that the increase in oil prices following recent upsets in the Gulf region would lead to higher heating oil prices, which in turn would lead to a rise in the consumer index overall.
While heating oil rose by 38.8 percent, overall energy prices did not leap by as much as might have been expected in the month, increasing only 1.3 percent.
"Higher mineral oil prices helped push rates up," said Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt.

"But the rise in mineral oil prices is not worrying at the moment. We have seen the bottom...for inflation rates, and they could begin edging higher again very, very slowly in the coming months," said Grebe.

This was not something to get overly worried about, however, said Grebe. "On the mineral oil prices, we expect that the winter will not be so very severe and that higher prices will not have a huge impact on the overall index."

Bond market traders said the numbers were exactly in line with expectations and were unphased by higher petroleum prices. The figures failed to move the market appreciably, and the overall trend was sideways.
One senior Bund trader in Frankfurt said: "Right now the inflation data is still supporting Bundesbank policy of holding short-term rates steady."
